Sponsor: Get 10% off Squarespace purchases (https://geni.us/BqEpf)
This review of the NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU benchmarks its performance vs. the AMD RX 7600, RX 6700 XT, NVIDIA RTX 4060 Ti, Intel Arc A750, and plenty more modern cards. We also included benchmarks and comparisons against the RTX 3060, RTX 2060, and even the GTX 1060 to help you determine if it's time to upgrade. The 4060 isn't as poorly positioned as the 4060 Ti -- that one was really bad positioning -- but it still feels like the relative performance would equate a "4050" by traditional naming.

@ I was confused too at first. HWinfo reported the 50W sensor, and the card was idling above 40C! But then I installed MSI afterburner, and noticed the fans weren't running when idle, lol. With a new fan-profile, the idle temperature dropped to 6C above ambient. Clearly the core is not using 50W ...

Under load, the 50W sensor goes up by exactly the same amount as the normal power sensor. Maybe the reading comes from the very same sensor, and the coders simply forgot to remove some old lines of code?

=======

I also made a low power profile, by capping the voltage to 0.890V. This is very nice for an old game like Fallout 4 on ultra settings. The core only uses 29W, with a maximum temperature of 41C and the fans at 1700 RPM (50%). The 4060 may not be the fastest card, but it's extremely efficient on a 1080p system.

Just ignore the bogus sensor. :)

The more I think about GDDR7 I also worry that Nvidia might decide to put 12gb's of 24gbps GDDR7 (good) over a 96-bit bus (bad) for 320GB/s total bandwidth (landing between a 4060 and 3060🤦‍♂). Tl;dr next-gen memory should help quite a bit. Just beware of even more cutdown dies.

comments.text:
They might not want people to own a card for 4 years, but their own internal numbers show that for a 60 class owner they are upgrading roughly every 3 to 5 years... *if they upgrade at all*. That last bit is what this is all about, and something you seem to be failing to take into the equation.

The most telling info to come out of Nvidia was what a lot of us already knew: The vast majority of gamers are still using something older than a 3060. The question is why? Price? Economics? FPS per dollar? No, none of that even occurs or matters to most gamers. They just want to play the game, and they can, and that's all that matters to them.

It's simply there is no reason to upgrade. If you've only ever played at 720p or 1080p, you don't even know the difference, and so don't care. If you've only ever played games at 30 FPS, you don't know your missing anything, and the fact is if you're used to those kind of settings, when you try a newer game? You're going to get more of the same as the game will lower its settings to fit your needs. So you will never need to upgrade until a game comes along that literally won't play on your card. Which don't really exist...

It's not about trying to get positive PR or good feedback. It's been 3 plus years of Nvidia must die from Youtube, and it's done nothing to their numbers. Sure sales are down, but they are also down for AMD and everyone else, so that argument holds zero value, and is beginning to sound more like arrogance than logic. What was it Linus said? "It's how the game works, you release a good product, we give a good review, and people buy it, if not, well then maybe next time". That statement was the height of Youtube hubris, and is kind of repeated across the major channels in various different forms. No, it's not about Youtube and it's 1-2 million views of that kind of subject matter, it's about a potential market of around 100 million consumers out there that are still on 1060s or something similar.

That is why the prices are dropping so fast: They are desperately trying to get those users. Nvidia/AMD/Intel all want this group of buyers more than any other because they are the path to increased profitability, not the existing buyers. Those buyers are already locked in, and will be buying something no matter what. Despite what you guys like to push, they honestly don't care if you buy a 4060 or 3060 or even cross brands to buy a 6700XT or A770, it doesn't matter, it means you are engaged and buying. Which means you are a potential profit avenue for them in the future. The vast majority of gamers not buying anything since 2016? They are the real target.

Edit: This particular push is targeted also at the 2060 owners, this is around the time they'd be looking to upgrade. It'll be another two years for the 5060, so it's likely they'll jump now if ever.

comments.text:
With Nvidia causing issues with their own products and AMD being lackluster this release cycle, it could be interesting in what we see from Intel between improved drivers, Alchemist +, and the release of Battlemage.  Assuming next year's releases are also disappointing, Intel might have a great run up into actually being competitive with Arc, and hopefully will incentivize them to make better cards and widen their product range in the future. 

Although, I'm still not happy with the state of RT and AI-based upscaling, especially the former.  I still hold the opinion that RT should be a separate card until everything is good enough for it to be seamlessly integrated into the main card at the point that even the low-end has decent performance; just like PhysX was way back in the day as an add-in solution.  I'm now holding that opinion for tools like FSR and DLSS, and whatever Intel eventually puts out, and especially for hardware solutions like DLSS, an add-in card could easily be brand-agnostic, AMD's solution could be pushed onto better hardware, etc.  And I get it, lanes are limited, the new high end cards are behemoths, etc., but until all of this can be shoehorned into low-end and even non-performance multimedia cards, then the solution being pushed should be at the customer's will to opt into the tech rather than having things shoved down our throats in the most half-baked way possible, especially when the card itself has basic struggles like memory bandwidth; the current solution just does not work well outside of the highest end.  I would rather co-process things than rely on a half-assed chunk of silicon, give us more die real estate with actual base performance than trying to shoehorn everything into one cramped chip.  Anyone with half a braincell could've seen this coming when the RT craze first started gaining traction, same with the situation where upscaling is so heavily relied on for performance, which is why these things need to be off-die as a separate chip, whether that's a separate card entirely or multiple chips on the same card, co-processing until everything is good enough for basic consumer cards to handle with decent performance is the only way to properly ramp up into a single-die solution.  Give it a few more generations and a single-die solution at this product tier might make sense, but then again this has been in the development pipeline for how many years now; hint, we're coming up on the five year release of an RTX series card, and they have yet to figure out the lower end of performance cards, this is why a single-die solution doesn't currently make sense.

comments.text:
For those arguing RTX4060 or Ti is "mid-range" when its 8GB VRAM is so limiting: 1080p even at ultra settings is NOT midrange in 2023! There are plenty of people who're playing at 4K ULTRA now (high end), so "mid-range" now would be 1440p ULTRA settings with playable FPS and no glitches! Logically this means that basic entry level (budget) gaming in 2023 STARTS at 1080p ULTRA settings with smooth FPS and zero glitches - a 8GB VRAM graphics card CANNOT manage that even with all CURRENT games, with upcoming games planning on needing even more VRAM!

An 8GB VRAM GPU in 2023 is a 720p card, which is a resolution and performance which was long in the tooth a decade ago and should be dead and buried before now! We need to move on and allow games companies to put "16GB VRAM" on the GPU for MINIMUM required specs to play the game without NVidia and AMD shortsightedly and greedily holding them back! Doubling VRAM from 8GB to 16GB only costs $20 more but makes a MASSIVE difference!

Another point: low VRAM is making MUCH bigger game installations (150GB not unusual) because it has to include crappy low resolution textures, as well as photorealistic textures for those with enough VRAM, to allow MIPMAPPING, which increases used drive space by a huge 33%! Aim for a GPU with 16GB VRAM or more, even if that means switching to AMD as high VRAM graphics makes a MUCH bigger difference than fake extra filler frames that cause latency by NVidia!

comments.text:
First of, thank you for great work! I have a proposal for an additional segment in your videos, for which testing should not be too difficult: idle power consumption of CPUs and GPUs.

I live in Germany with electricity currently costing 0.44€/kWh

I am probably not speaky only for myself when I say that most of the time using my computer not spent gaming or on productivity, but on mundane tasks such as browsing the internet, watching videos, looking and moving files and other such activities that consume close to no power.
I am therefore very interested in the idle power consumption of different products.

For example, my ...

i9 12900 consumed 9W idle
r9 5900X consumed 40W idle
3080 consumes 90W idle

there are things that would have been very good to know beforehand.

These 40W + 90W add up to 130W, which is more or less what I measured going into the PSU (~145W idle)


What does this cost compared to a ~10W idle 1060 6GB and a ~10W 13500?


Assuming a PSU loss of 50% at low power, this would be a comparison between 145W and 40W idle. Thats ~100W idle difference.

100W = 0.1kW
My computer runs idle for about 8 hours a day (I am a remote university student)

0.1 kW * 365,25 days/year * 8 h/day * 0.44€/kWh = 128,57€/year IDLE power consumption.

I believe this is something one should be able to factor in when purchasing a product and getting this information is currently very difficult.

comments.text:
@THU31  I guess the performance drop for the 6500XT (another x8 card) going from PCIe 4.0 to 3.0 being anywhere between 10% to 20% was our lack of understanding.
If you cut the number of lanes in half, you cut the potential bandwidth in half. PCIe 4.0 x16 won't bottleneck any of these cards, PCIe 3.0 x16 and PCIe 4.0 x8 will be the same and unnoticeably worse than the former, but PCIe 3.0 x8 will be a quarter of the bandwidth and will definitely impact performance enough to change the value proposition. And that's the issue here, a "budget" (formerly midrange...) card is more likely to be used in a system limited to PCIe 3.0, giving it x8 lanes handicaps it for the casual user who doesn't know better, since it won't show up in most benchmarks or be explained in any vendor datasheet.
Also, as an aside, don't condescend to random strangers on the internet without doing the legwork.
TLDR: PCIe 3.0 x8 bottlenecks even a 6500XT and the proof is within a mouseclick's reach.

comments.text:
As per several different dictionaries
Low end is defined as the products at the lower cost of a given product family(the lower third price).
Examples of low end cards
RTX 4060, RTX 4060TI, and RTX 4070
There is no dollar ammount that defines low end.
What defines low end, is the price difference between the most expensive, and least expensive product a company makes within a given brand, say Geforce instead of Quadro or Tesla,
So if the lowest end card is $299, and the highest end card is $1600, and there are many cards in between, you basically take that $1300 price difference, cut it into equal 3rds, then anything that falls into the lower third is low end middle third is mid range, and upper third is high end, so from $299 to $732 is by definition low end, from $732 to 1165 is mid range, and from $1165 to $1600 is high end
comments.author: @denvera1g1

comments.text:
Now low end is not restricted to only one company, and only one product stack within a company, but without setting your parameters that is the default
For instance, if you say the 4070 is low end, it is assumed you are talking only about the Geforce RTX 4000 series of cards.
But, if you set your parameters before hand, say for example, Of all past cards, the $600 RTX 4070 is high end because the GTX 1080 was $600, and the Radeon VII was $700 is equally as valid as saying the 4070 is a low end RTX 4000 series card

comments.text:
They're trying to further segment their "gamer" users from their "enterprise" (AI) users; this is why Nvlink is no longer available on geforce cards, as well as why Nvidia has been so stingy with the VRAM lately - they want to setup the paradigm that "gamers don't need much VRAM, whereas professional users (who are willing to pay a lot more money) do. Nvidia can't sell their $100k AI cards if customers can get the same performance at a fraction of the cost by buying a couple of Geforce cards, so they've nerfed the hell out of em.

"Oh, you want what is essentially a 4090 but with 48GB (~$50) of VRAM? That'll be $7000."

They want to charge their big AI customers as much as possible, and to do they they're screwing gamers out of the 16GB of VRAM we need.

In the big data processing/AI world, there's a massive advantage to having a ton of VRAM available to a single GPU. Often times it's the difference between a dataset fitting entirely in VRAM vs needing to be split up and re-aggregated later.

Unlike many other workloads, AI doesn't really care that much about where it's being trained/run. If Nvidia didn't artificially restrict the 4090's capabilities in that area, it'd be much more cost-effectively to use Geforce cards rather than expensive AI cards. Nvidia doesn't want that - they wanna charge 5x more for the same product, and who can blame em?

A 16GB 4070 Ti would be an excellent card. I'm driving 1440p/165hz displays from a 4090, and you can do stuff like play Path-Traced Cyberpunk @ 100-144fps (DLSS3 on).

It's sad but there's no more-reasonably valued card that can do that right now. 4090 @ 1440p is actually the best gaming experience you can get today, and that's kinda pathetic.

I am really grateful that GN spent more thn 3 words on the power efficiency argument this time. But i still don't think it made a lot of sense. "At this price point users don't generally care about power consumption" 10s later - "At the higher price points consumption is shamelessly off the charts anyway!!!" - so which is it? Who DOES actually care about power consumption? The people buying a 4060 or the people buying a 4090? Maybe it's the poeple buying a 4070? But this GPU is still 600$ MSRP...which is double from the 4060. So is GN really suggesting that you have to spend 600$+ before you should care about high electricity costs? Frankly, that's absurd. And yes, i am from Germany. Thanks for including our power prices this time.

Secondly: GN accuses GPU manufacturers to be "stuck in 2016" with the 1080p res. But they themselves seem to be stuck there as well. Have you checked average summer temperatures in Europe over the last decade? I can tell you one thing: This 21 °C room temperature is a JOKE. People who buy "budget GPUs" will not spend thousands of dollars on air conditioning or professional cooling solutions. They just won't. Air conditioning is a LOT more uncommon in Europe than it is in the US and our currently exorbitant power prices mean it won't get any more common, either. I live i southern Germany. My average room temperature over the last month was ~26 °C daytime. If i lived in Spain, you could very well make that a 36 °C. And we are still a good ways from the hottest period of the year. You stated in your 7600 XT review that it runs too hot at 21 °C - wich means it will either throttle down, BSD or just flat out DIE in a room at 26 °C+ with sub-optimal case ventilation (which budget gamers are more likely to have than somebody buying a 4090). ​​​ @rhoharane nce you start thinking about TDP you can look into what Mobile/Quadro does with the clocks/cores.  They usually run a card with more cores at a lower clock speed.  The power consumption and heat gets way better and the performance is still good.  For example you can get a 1080 yourself and lower the clocks until the fps/watt is much better.  Or a Quadro P4000/P5000 (Or A4000+) where they do that for you and bin the chips accordingly.  Since it runs cooler the fan isn't running as fast, and the case doesn't need as much airflow and the PSU isn't dumping as much.  Its all a trickle down.  If you don't mind AMD I snagged a 5700 for $123, it is pretty nice.  Although if you have PCIe 4.0 a 6600 with x8 PCIe is even better on power consumption because there are less lanes to run.

Same as hot rodding cars.  Some people like an 1,100lb Yamaha/Suzuki powered Lotus 7.  Some get a 4,000LB Dodge Charger or Camaro even though the power/weight is the same as the smaller cars.  I'd probably tend more to the Miata/Lotus side.
